aircraft departs a prepared surface: Aircraft Departs Prepared Surface / Emergency Ground Egress

overview: This event consolidates earlier pattern and emergency skills into a more complete crosswind and runway-emergency brief. You should be ready to explain how you will adjust the pattern for a crosswind, when an abort becomes mandatory, what changes once the aircraft departs the prepared surface, and how windshear or a UFCP failure can turn a normal pattern into a waveoff or recovery problem.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Crosswind work here is less about learning a new technique and more about setting the picture early enough that you never end up chasing lineup late.

children.text: Before takeoff, note wind direction from tower and the windsock so you already know which controls will be in as the roll starts.
Start with aileron into the wind, reduce that input as speed builds, and use rudder to stop weathervaning and keep the nose aligned with the runway.
Rotate firmly at takeoff speed so the aircraft does not skip sideways off the upwind wheel, then level the wings and crab into the wind after liftoff.
Carry a crab on downwind as needed to hold the proper track, then use a wing-low final so drift is gone before touchdown.
In the approach turn, adjust bank and power early enough to avoid overshooting or undershooting final.
On final and through the flare, keep the upwind wing down, align the nose with rudder, and increase aileron as the airplane slows.

For full stops, touchdown should be on the upwind main first and crosswind controls stay in through rollout. For touch-and-goes, hold the crosswind picture through the ground roll and rotate at 90 KIAS.
Wave off if more than 45 degrees of bank is required or if side motion, drift, or crab remain unresolved.
In gusty conditions, add one-half the gust factor to final approach speed, but no more than 10 knots.
Brakes are for directional help only after the aircraft is below 80 KIAS and fully settled on the runway.
Common traps are too little aileron at the start of the roll, failing to reduce aileron as speed builds, holding a crab into touchdown, and trying to salvage a bad picture instead of waving off.

items.text: An abort is for any abnormal or unsafe condition before max abort speed, but the priority never changes: keep the airplane under control first, then stop it on the remaining runway.

children.text: Abort cues include blown tires, smoke or fuel leak, fire or chip indications, rising ITT, fluctuating oil pressure, bird strike, obstacles, or any malfunction that makes the takeoff unsafe to continue.
Immediate actions are PCL to IDLE and brakes as required while maintaining directional control with rudder and nosewheel steering.
Call the abort over ICS per local SOP, but do not let radio work get ahead of keeping the airplane straight.
Maximum braking is one smooth, increasing application as the aircraft slows. Do not pump or slam the brakes.
Above 80 KIAS, braking is less effective because lift is still unloading the wheels, so be cautious about aggressive pedal input and watch for directional-control problems.
If directional control is being lost, release braking immediately and reapply cautiously once the airplane is straight again.
If you have to cross a lowered BAK-15 during the stop, release the brakes before passing it and resume braking once clear.

items.text: N/W/C focus: There is no anti-skid, so do not brake before full weight is on wheels. After maximum-effort braking, do not set the parking brake or taxi into a congested area until the brakes cool, and do not request the barrier.
If the aircraft is about to depart, or has already departed, the prepared surface, stop trying to save the rollout and transition immediately to shutdown and egress decisions.

children.text: Execute Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground with PCL OFF and FIREWALL SHUTOFF HANDLE PULL.
Emergency Ground Egress is then as required based on fire, traffic, terrain, or aircraft damage.
Do not try to steer back onto the runway once you are off. After engine shutdown, nosewheel steering is gone, so any remaining directional control comes from braking only.
ISS mode selector to SOLO.
Install both seat safety pins before egress.
Set the parking brake as required and open the canopy if possible.

If the canopy cannot be opened or right-side egress is required, remove both CFS handle safety pins, rotate and pull both CFS handles, then release upper fittings, lower fittings, and leg restraint garters before exiting.
After the crew is clear, turn BAT, GEN, and AUX BAT OFF if time and situation allow.
Once clear of the aircraft, move away at a 45-degree angle off the tail and rally 300 feet from the aircraft while staying alert for emergency vehicles.

items.text: Warning-focused note: If the canopy fracturing system and canopy latch both fail, ejection may be the only remaining way out. Ensure oxygen mask on and visor down before actuating CFS.

sections.title: Aircraft Departs Prepared Surface / Emergency Ground Egress

items.text: Windshear should be avoided if possible, but once it is part of the picture the goal is to protect margin early instead of reacting late to the airspeed loss.

children.text: Treat thunderstorms, gust fronts, virga, LLWAS alerts, PIREPs, and recent frontal passages as cues to slow down the plan or avoid the approach or takeoff entirely.
Use the longest suitable runway, takeoff flaps, and delay rotation up to 10 knots above normal if windshear is suspected on takeoff.
After liftoff, maintain the proper climb attitude instead of chasing airspeed, and do not accelerate past normal climb speed until clear of the shear.
On approach, use takeoff flaps, fly up to 10 knots fast, and be stabilized by 1000 feet AGL.
If windshear is encountered on approach, execute an immediate go-around or waveoff.
Do not chase every airspeed change with large trim or power swings. Expect the wind gradient to change what the aircraft is doing as you descend.
Severe windshear is roughly a 15-knot airspeed change or 500 FPM vertical-speed change; that is your reminder to treat it as a real hazard, not a nuisance.

items.text: A UFCP failure is manageable, but it takes away the normal quick path for radio, nav, transponder, and baro changes. The fix is to transition calmly to the MFD NAV page and land as soon as practical.

children.text: First, check the UFCP circuit breaker and reset it if it is open.
Use ALT BARO on the NAV page to change the barometric setting, and ALT CNS to adjust COM, NAV, and transponder settings through the scratchpad and line-select keys.
From the frequency page you can also control transponder mode and altitude reporting without the UFCP.
The MFD NAV page is the backup path; these shortcuts are not available from the TSD page.

items.text: Know what you lose with the failure as well: FMS execute, Mag/True toggle, GS/CAS/TAS HUD speed toggle, and normal radio tuning through the UFCP are unavailable to the cockpit with the failed unit.
